# How I Optimized SEO for a Next.js Portfolio Site Without Breaking Build Performance

I built a portfolio with Next.js 14 App Router, deployed to Vercel. The first week of traffic was under 10 visits per day. I knew something was wrong with how search engines saw the site. The problem was not a single bug but a set of small misconfigurations that kept my pages from ranking.

## Why SEO matters for developer portfolios

Search engines are the first place most potential clients find a freelancer. If a page is missing a title tag, a description, or a structured data snippet, Google will not surface it. I also discovered that duplicate content from static pages and blog posts caused crawl budget waste. Fixing these issues gave me a clear path to more visibility.

## Common pitfalls I hit in the first build

### Missing meta tags

I had a global layout that did not inject a `<title>` or `<meta name="description">`. The result was blank titles in search results and a generic description that did not reflect the page content.

### Duplicate content

The blog was built with a static site generator, but I also exposed the same content via API routes for a headless CMS. Search engines indexed both URLs, causing duplicate pages and confusing the indexer.

### Slow hydration

The page bundle included heavy third-party scripts that ran on the client. The hydration time pushed the First Contentful Paint (FCP) beyond the recommended 2.5 seconds, and Google penalised the page for performance.

## My step-by-step optimization

### Use Next.js Head component

I replaced the global layout with a custom `Head` component that receives props from each page. I set a default title and description, then overrode them where needed. This gave every page a unique snippet without extra code.

### Server-side rendering for blog posts

I switched the blog pages from static generation to server-side rendering (SSR). SSR ensures that each request receives fresh meta tags and that the content is available to crawlers before JavaScript runs. I kept static generation for the home page where the content rarely changes.

### Image optimization

Next.js’ `next/image` automatically optimises images. I set `priority` on hero images and used `fill` for responsive backgrounds. The image sizes dropped from 2 MB to 400 KB on average, and Lighthouse scores improved.

### Structured data

I added JSON-LD for `BlogPosting` and `Person` schemas on relevant pages. The code was a simple object that I stringified and inserted into the `<Head>`. Google recognised my author profile and the blog content, boosting relevance.

### Canonical URLs

I added `<link rel="canonical" href="https://myportfolio.com/blog/slug" />` to every blog post. This told search engines which URL to index, eliminating duplicate content.

### Sitemaps

I generated a sitemap using `next-sitemap`. The XML file lists all pages and is automatically uploaded to Vercel’s `public` folder. Google Search Console picks it up on the first crawl.

### Performance budgets

I set a maximum bundle size of 200 KB for the home page and 300 KB for other pages. I used `next-bundle-analyzer` to monitor the size after each commit. When the bundle exceeded the budget, I refactored or removed unnecessary dependencies.

## Production debugging

### Vercel logs

I enabled `VERCEL_LOGS` and filtered for 404 and 500 errors. The logs revealed that a mis-named image path caused a 404 on the blog page, which I fixed by adding a fallback.

### Lighthouse audits

After each change I ran `next build && next export && lighthouse https://myportfolio.com`. The audit highlighted improvements in performance, accessibility, and SEO. I tracked the SEO score from 65 to 92 over three iterations.

### Real User Monitoring

I added `next-analytics` to capture real-user metrics. The data showed that the average load time dropped from 4.2 s to 2.8 s after the optimisations. Users stayed longer and clicked through to my contact page.

## Result and metrics

### Traffic increase

Within a month of deploying the changes, organic traffic grew from 8 visits per day to 45 visits per day. The bounce rate dropped from 70 % to 48 %. These numbers came from Google Analytics and were consistent across devices.

### Crawl errors resolved

Google Search Console reported zero crawl errors after the canonical and sitemap fixes. The index coverage report moved from “Excluded” to “Valid” for all blog posts.

## Lessons learned

- **Start with the basics**: Meta tags, canonical URLs, and a sitemap are low-effort fixes that deliver high impact.
- **Keep the bundle lean**: A small bundle improves both performance and SEO, because faster pages rank higher.
- **Test in production**: Vercel logs and Lighthouse audits are essential to catch issues that do not appear in local builds.

## FAQ

**Q: Do I need a dedicated SEO tool?**
A: Not for a small portfolio. The built-in tools in Next.js and Vercel cover most needs.

**Q: How often should I update the sitemap?**
A: Every time you add or remove a page. Automating with `next-sitemap` keeps it up to date.

**Q: Can I use a CMS for the blog?**
A: Yes, but make sure the CMS routes are not duplicated by static pages. Use canonical tags or disable the CMS route for crawlers.

**Bottom line**

Optimising SEO on a Next.js portfolio is a series of small, repeatable steps. By fixing meta tags, avoiding duplicate content, and monitoring performance, I raised traffic and reduced bounce rate without adding extra build time. The same approach works for any developer site that wants to be found by the right audience.
